items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1972-05-27
items.q: Cootie picked this up from Chris Kelly

ctx.x: Well, what was it like on the other side? Beautiful.

I can remember the trees and the green shrubbery. A few homes. Beautiful homes sitting in these, under these great big trees. Of course, you had the slum area over there. Well, now I wouldn't say slum. I hate to use it. Yeah. But, for instance, Buddy B.T. lived in the great trumpet players about 25, 30 years ahead of time. He lived in the little one room shack and he took a vacuum to me. And every time I would go to the dock, I'd try to see how fast I could get off of that. And we'd sit down and talk with Buddy.…
One of the things I was trying to get in there from a slant and vicular way as a country.

items.title: Don Albert Interview, 1961-06-06
items.q: later on whether they say it or not, Cootie Williams adopted what he was doing with the Flushy.

ctx.x: Do you remember anything about his style? Like you know, was he a high note man?

No, not a high note man. In those days trumpet players didn't play high notes. They had more of a running style. You mentioned the trumpet player the other day, Punch. Punch Miller. Do you remember Punch Miller? Sure. Well Punch Miller to me is as near to playing the style that Buddy played than anybody else that I heard. A style similar to what he's playing. Now Punch, don't misunderstand me, now Punch isn't copying Buddy PT. He's playing his style. But he gives you an idea what Buddy actually played. Oh he was…
Oh, there's something else that I told you I saw, I was talking to Emmanuel Sales the other day.
